state.claim: Fact check: Harris' statement on Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination misses key details

records.title: Kamala Harris, Honest Abe and the Supreme Court
records.retrieval_query: What exactly did Kamala Harris say about Abraham Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination, and when and where did she say it?

passages.P1: **Q: Was Sen. Kamala Harris’ story at the vice presidential debate about President Abraham Lincoln’s 1864 Supreme Court vacancy correct?**
passages.P2: **A: There’s no evidence that Lincoln said he delayed the nomination to let voters choose the next president, as Harris said.**
passages.P4: Last night in the VP debate Kamala Harris notes that Abraham Lincoln chose to delay nomination of a SCOTUS until after the election, because it was the right thing to do. Is this accurate?
passages.P6: At the vice presidential debate, Sen. Kamala Harris invoked a bit of Civil War-era history by offering the purported words of “Honest Abe” about filling a Supreme Court vacancy just before a presidential election. The tale was intended to bolster Democrats’ argument that the current Supreme Court vacancy should be filled by the winner of the 2020 election.
passages.P7: Many readers have asked us whether her story about President Abraham Lincoln holds up.
passages.P8: While Harris got the basic facts about the timing of the vacancy, she attributed an unsubstantiated quote to the 16th president and advanced an unproven claim about his motivations.
passages.P10: > **Harris, Oct. 7:** In 1864, one of the, I think political heroes, certainly the President, I assume of you also, Mr. Vice President, is Abraham Lincoln. Abraham Lincoln was up for reelection and it was 27 days before the election. And a seat became open on the United States Supreme Court. Abraham Lincoln’s party was in charge, not only of the White House, but the Senate. But Honest Abe said it’s not the right thing to do. The American people deserve to make the decision about who will be the next president of the United States. And then that person can select who will serve for a lifetime on the highest court of our land.
passages.P11: It’s true that a Supreme Court vacancy occurred just 27 days before the 1864 election, when Chief Justice Robert B. Taney died on Oct. 12. Taney was known for offering the decision in the 1857 Dred Scott case, which had declared that Black people, slaves or free, were not U.S. citizens.
passages.P12: And it’s true that, while Lincoln’s Republican party controlled the Senate, he didn’t make a nomination until after he was reelected. Lincoln nominated Salmon Chase for chief justice in December 1864. Chase had served as Lincoln’s Treasury secretary and had vied for the Republican presidential nomination against Lincoln in 1860.
passages.P13: But Lincoln’s exact rationale for waiting to nominate Chase until after the election isn’t clear — and there is no record of him making a quote that squares with the one Harris described — according to historians.
passages.P14: “Lincoln never actually explained the delay in his own words, so we don’t know his motivation,” Christian McWhirter, Lincoln Historian at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, told us in an email.
passages.P15: McWhirter continued: “History is, of course, all about interpretation, so historians have mostly relied on context to draw conclusions. The 1864 election is certainly important context, as is the fact that the Senate was out of session until December 5. Things like that can provide clues for what Lincoln might have been thinking, but ultimately we can never know exactly.”

records.title: Harris jumped to conclusions on Lincoln's court nomination
records.retrieval_query: What exactly did Kamala Harris say about Abraham Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination, and when and where did she say it?

passages.P1: # Kamala Harris jumped to conclusions about Abraham Lincoln’s delayed Supreme Court nomination
passages.P7: • Lincoln was faced with a Supreme Court vacancy 27 days before Election Day in 1864, when his party controlled the Senate. He decided to wait until after winning the election to pursue the nomination.
passages.P8: • However, historians who have studied the relationship between Lincoln and his nominee, Salmon P. Chase, said that Lincoln’s decision may have stemmed from political or logistical reasons rather than high-minded reasons.
passages.P9: See the sources for this story
passages.P10: Democratic vice presidential candidate Kamala Harris invoked Abraham Lincoln to say why a nominee to succeed the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg should not be confirmed until the next president is sworn in.
passages.P11: Harris brought a “history lesson” to the vice presidential debate on Oct. 7. Harris said that Lincoln was up for reelection when the chief justice, Roger Taney, died on Oct. 12, 1864, which was just 27 days before the election.
passages.P12: “Honest Abe said it’s not the right thing to do. The American people deserve to make the decision about who will be the next president of the United States, and then that person can select who will serve for a lifetime on the highest court of our land,” Harris said. “And so (Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden) and I are very clear: The American people are voting right now, and it should be their decision about who will serve on this most important body for a lifetime.”
passages.P13: Harris was right about the proximity of Taney’s death to the election; it was 27 days ahead of the election, the shortest in history. Ginsburg, by contrast, died 46 days before the election. Lincoln did not seek confirmation of his nominee, Salmon P. Chase, until after the election.
passages.P14: However, it’s hard to confirm that Lincoln’s motivations in waiting until after the election were as high-minded as Harris said.
passages.P15: We couldn’t find any evidence for Lincoln saying what Harris described. Michael Burlingame, the distinguished chair in Lincoln studies at the University of Illinois-Springfield, told PolitiFact, “I’ve never seen anything like that quote in all my 36 years of Lincoln research.”
passages.P17: Chase had until recently been serving as Lincoln’s Treasury secretary, and was at times considered a political rival to Lincoln, but one he respected. Chase was also respected among anti-slavery Republicans in the Senate, and was ultimately confirmed him by a unanimous vote.
passages.P18: Lincoln “knew Chase to be consistently loyal to his own principles, especially in his attitude toward slavery and the rights of the Black man,” wrote Susan J. Court in a 1981 journal article.
passages.P19: This perspective marked a sharp contrast with the chief justice he was replacing. Taney had been the author of the Dred Scott decision, which ruled that enslaved people could not be treated as citizens with full rights.
passages.P20: But while Lincoln did delay the nomination until Dec. 6, which was weeks after the election, not all historians consider his motivations for doing so to be clear.
passages.P21: The Biden campaign pointed PolitiFact to a tweet during the debate by historian Michael Beschloss that said, “Harris is correct that when Roger Taney died in October 1864, Abraham Lincoln deferred a Supreme Court appointment until after election so that next President, with a new mandate, could do it.”

passages.P1: # Fact check: Harris' statement on Lincoln's Supreme Court nomination misses key details
passages.P2: ## The claim: Harris' story about why Lincoln waited to fill a vacancy on the Supreme Court is wrong.
passages.P3: The question of when the late-Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat will be filled by a nominee of the president's choosing was up for debate immediately after her death last month. It was an unavoidable topic during the first vice presidential debate on Oct. 7.
passages.P4: President Donald Trump has officially nominated 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Amy Coney Barrett, a noted conservative, to the Supreme Court, USA TODAY reported. Barrett's confirmation would give the court a 6-3 conservative majority. Confirmation hearings began on Oct. 12, 22 days before the Nov. 3 presidential election.
passages.P5: During the debate, Vice President Mike Pence asked whether Sen. Kamala Harris and Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden would increase the number of justices, if they win the election.
passages.P6: Harris responded with a story about President Abraham Lincoln's decision to delay a court nomination until after his 1864 campaign.
passages.P7: "Abraham Lincoln was up for reelection, and it was 27 days before the election, and a seat became open on the United States Supreme Court. Abraham Lincoln's party was in charge, not only in the White House, but the Senate," Harris said. "But Honest Abe said, it's not the right thing to do. The American people deserve to make the decision about who will be the next president of the United States, and then that person can select who will serve for a lifetime on the highest court of our land."
passages.P8: It was a statement some disagreed with, including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich.
passages.P9: "Kamala Harris’ use of Lincoln to justify not nominating a Supreme Court Justice was totally false. The Senate was not in session and the minute it came into session Lincoln nominated a Justice. She is either really ignorant or just lied," Gingrich tweeted on Oct. 8.
passages.P10: A screenshot of the tweet was posted to Facebook that evening. The user who posted the screenshot did not respond to a request comment from USA TODAY.
passages.P11: Other social media posts similarly claimed Harris' story was wrong.
passages.P12: Indeed, Harris' history lesson on Lincoln missed key details.
passages.P13: ## Did Lincoln delay filling a seat on the Supreme Court?
passages.P14: Presidential historian Michael Beschloss tweeted on the night of the debate that Harris was right.
passages.P15: "Harris is correct that when Roger Taney died in October 1864, Abraham Lincoln deferred a Supreme Court appointment until after election so that next President, with a new mandate, could do it, Beschloss said.
passages.P16: Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, most famous for his majority opinion in the 1857 Dred Scott v. Sandford case, in which he wrote Black people were "so far inferior, that they had no rights that the white man was bound to respect; and that the negro might justly and lawfully be reduced to slavery for his own benefit," died on Oct. 12, 1864, 27 days before the Nov. 8 election, as Harris cited.
passages.P17: But other evidence points to Lincoln being a savvy politician instead of a populist by deciding to delay a nomination for Taney's replacement before a major election.
